newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Stone age gets computerised to serve conservation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Stone age gets computerised to serve conservation.

text.p: Scattered across the vastness of the Kalahari desert, a handful of Bushmen survive who can read the tracks of reptile, lion or antelope with the ease of a Western teenager surfing the Internet.

Now South African Louis Liebenberg is harnessing the ancient skills of hunter-gatherers to state-of-the-art computers in a plan that he says can help the survival of both the Bushmen and the world's wildlife.

He has started a pilot project in one of South Africa's national parks for trackers on the park staff to carry hand-held computers into which they enter data on the animal signs they see during patrols.

"It's a pen-based computer, and we've developed an interface that illiterate trackers can use based on little pictures and icons. The tracker just touches the screen with a pen," Liebenberg said in an interview.

The theory is that the computers will allow trackers to record information that would otherwise be quickly lost but now can be used by wildlife managers to combat poachers and assess the health of plant and animal populations.
"The computer covers a full range of species, down to different mongoose species," Liebenberg said.
"You can count the number of adults, of females, of juveniles. The computer is connected to a GPS (global positioning system) which automatically pinpoints the position and time and the date.
"So it's a very specific observation which at the end of the day, when you've gathered vast amounts of data, you can analyse statistically."
Liebenberg said skilled trackers could identify individual black rhinos from the pattern of cracks on the underside of their feet. "It's like a fingerprint."
The tracker can follow the trail of a rhino, noting the animal's activities along the way, such as how much it ate and what kind of vegetation.
"This has management implications in the sense that you can do the same with, for example, kudu (antelope), and determine what is the competition for food between rhino and kudu," Liebenberg said.
"You get a much better idea of whether there are too many rhino or if you've got space for more."
He said the system would for the first time provide accurate data on nocturnal species which were seldom picked up by current wildlife surveys conducted from aircraft.

"There's an enormous amount of new information that becomes available. It could form the very basis of conservation management and for the cost of 10 hours of helicopter flying time you can employ a tracker for a whole year in the field...
"If it works here, I think it could revolutionise wildlife management throughout the world."

Liebenberg said the value of the system depended on the skills of the trackers using it, but he estimated that possibly no more than 100 highly skilled Bushmen trackers still survived in southern Africa.
"There's a level of refinement that you find among traditional hunter-gatherers that you simply don't find elsewhere," he said.
"You're looking at tracking as a tradition that goes back hundreds of thousands of years, and you're reaching a point where your last bow and arrow hunters are disappearing very rapidly."
He believes his system could give the art of tracking a new importance and respectability that would help those who practise it.

"You're creating jobs for members of the local community using indigenous African skills that can also be important for tourism, because if you know where the animals are, you know where to take the tourists."
Liebenberg hopes the computer project will provide evidence to support a theory he developed, while a student of physics and philosophy, that stone age tracking was the origin of modern science.

"It's always been assumed that science as we know it today was developed by the classical Greeks...But tracking involved the same hypothetico-deductive reasoning that is required in physics and mathematics."
Liebenberg compares a physicist making deductions about invisible particles from the signs they leave with a tracker forming theories about animal behaviour from the tracks of an antelope.
"There's a sort of cultural prejudice against people who are illiterate...But with a system like this, a tracker can make a significant scientific contribution in his own right.
"My big dream is, I want to see if I can get an illiterate tracker to submit a thesis to university."
